doc.title: David Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2022

title: Avant-garde players who skipped bebop; the Cookers' adventurous spirit
summary: Weiss says avant-garde musicians like Lester Bowie skipped bebop, praises Threadgill and Muhal Richard Abrams as composers, and says the Cookers carry an adventurous spirit and trust.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: I’m sorry, do they have the history of Ben Webster and before him?
Well that’s an interesting — that you chose Ben Webster — because I mean again, any time we talk this way we generalize and I’m going to get killed on something, but a lot of
the avante garde guys, as far as us, you know, swing, how we always analyze, I mean somebody analyzed it better than me and said, “Hey, they just skipped bebop.” You know?

The more avante garde guys, have you seen, they’re doing tributes to — you know Lester Bowie does Louis Armstrong. They come, I mean they skipped bebop. They took all the wonderful things about swing and that expressiveness and all the stuff those guys did, and they kind of continue on from there. That’s where they found their more emotional truth or their melodic sense or whatever it is they’re trying to do. I mean that’s one school of avante garde and it is the ones that are like the amazing composers, the ones that really interest me personally from what I come out of, like the Henry Threadgills and the Muhal Richard Abrams is guys who at least wrote incredible music. You know when it comes time to soloing, you know, but those are the guys that are writing the most interesting music I’m hearing over my career, the last twenty, thirty years. Henry Threadgill, Muhal Richard Abrams, I’m trying to think of who else. There’s got to be more than those. But that’s growth I like. But those guys come out of another thing, and they also come out of a classical thing. I mean Henry Threadgill lives around the corner. I talk to him all the time. He’s a Chicago guy. He talks about Gene Ammons all the time. You know? They know the music. So you’re in this thing like okay, I’m trying to do something more based in this, more advanced harmony, hopefully swing based, whatever, in that realm. But I want the adventurous spirit of these guys. You know? To keep looking. That’s what the Cookers I think grabs. Those guys came through everything, are well versed in everything and have always tried to push it a little forward. If you want it call it like the spiritual thing of the 70s or the more free thing of the 70s, or whatever. But whatever they’ve done is informed by George Cables with Dexter Gordon you know, Billy Harper with Max Roach. You know they came up through this stuff but it never was a limiting thing to them. You know, and Freddie Hubbard, that’s what he told me all the time it was like, “Man we tried stuff all the time. We never stopped trying things.” You know? I think sometimes better — those guys were so good they didn’t miss as much so it wasn’t apparent. You know? Or they missed better. I mean Billy Hart used to tell me some drummer used to tell him, “You recover better than anybody” and he didn’t know how to really take that. You know?

But it’s also true, I mean that’s another thing about the Cookers, we’ve played together enough, we know when somebody’s kind of going out on a limb a little bit, and they’ve got your back you know. They’re not going to let you crash and burn unless they’re mad at you or something. But that kind of trust goes a long way.
